replacement: 21. Where this kind of priestly medicine-mongering, the "guilty" kind, is concerned, every word of criticism is superfluous. As for the suggestion that emotional excess of this type, which in these cases the ascetic priest is eager to order for his sick patients (under the most sacred euphemism, as is obvious, and equally impregnated with the sanctity of his purpose), has ever really been of use to any sick man: who, if you please, would feel inclined to maintain such a proposition? At any rate, we should first come to an understanding about the expression "be of use." If you only mean that such a system of treatment has reformed man, I do not deny it. I merely add that to my mind "reformed" means as much as "tamed," "weakened," "discouraged," "refined," "daintified," "emasculated" (and so it means almost as much as injured). But when you are dealing mainly with sick, depressed and oppressed creatures, such a system, even granted that it makes the ill "better," always makes them more ill as well. Ask the mad-doctors what invariably results from a methodical application of penance-torture, contrition and salvation ecstasies. Ask history too. In every body politic where the ascetic priest has established this treatment of the sick, disease has each time spread with sinister speed through its whole length and breadth. What was always the "result"? A shattered nervous system on top of the existing malady, in the greatest as in the smallest, in individuals as in masses. The penance and redemption training gives us awful epileptic epidemics, the greatest known to history, such as the St. Vitus and St. John dances of the Middle Ages. Another phase of its after-effect is frightful mutilations and chronic depressions, which turn the temperament of a nation or a city (Geneva, Bale) once for all into its opposite. This training, again, is responsible for the witch-hysteria, a phenomenon analogous to somnambulism (eight great epidemic outbursts of this alone between 1564 and 1605). It also brings in its train those delirious death-cravings of large masses, whose awful "shriek," "evviva la morte!" was heard over the whole of Europe, interrupted now by voluptuous variations and now by a rage for destruction. Today the same emotional sequence, with the same intermittences and sudden changes, is observed universally wherever the ascetic doctrine of sin scores a great success once more (religious neurosis appears as a manifestation of the devil, there is no doubt of it. What is it? Quæritur). Speaking generally, the ascetic ideal and its sublime-moral cult, this most ingenious, reckless and perilous systematization of all methods of emotional excess, is written large in a dreadful and unforgettable fashion across the whole history of man, and unfortunately not only across history. I could scarcely name any other element that has done more destructive harm to the health and race efficiency of Europeans than this ideal. Without exaggeration, it can be called the real fatality in the history of the health of the European man. The most you can do is compare it with the specifically German influence: I mean the alcohol poisoning of Europe, which up to the present has kept pace exactly with the political and racial pre–dominance of the Germans (where they inoculated their blood, there too they inoculated their vice). Third in the series comes syphilis — magno sed proximo intervallo.
